title: Numeric Entry & Multiple-Answer
weightage: High — a few Numeric Entry and Multiple-Answer questions appear in every Quant section, and their formats trip up the unprepared
intro: Beyond the five-choice multiple-choice question and Quantitative Comparison, the GRE uses two answer formats that reward format-awareness as much as maths. Numeric Entry gives you no answer choices at all — you type the number into a box, or a numerator and denominator into a fraction box — so there is nothing to eliminate and no way to back-solve from options; your arithmetic must be exactly right. Multiple-Answer questions (officially "select one or more") can have any number of correct choices, from one to all of them, and you earn credit only if you mark every correct choice and no incorrect one — partial credit does not exist. This chapter covers the mechanics that quietly cost points: entering answers in the required form, telling a select-one from a select-all, checking every option deliberately, and using the on-screen basic calculator and estimation without burning time.

topics.name: Numeric Entry & Fraction Boxes
topics.details: A Numeric Entry question hands you an empty box instead of choices. That changes strategy fundamentally: you cannot eliminate wrong options or plug the choices back in, so you must actually solve and be precise. Two entry forms exist. A single box takes an integer or decimal, and it accepts a minus sign for negatives and a decimal point — if the answer is negative or a decimal, enter it as such. A fraction box gives you a numerator field and a denominator field; a helpful quirk is that you do not have to reduce — 6/8 is scored the same as 3/4 — so skip the simplification step to save time and avoid slips. Read the units and rounding instruction carefully: if the prompt says "to the nearest integer" or "in dollars", answer in exactly that form. Because there is no safety net of answer choices, a quick sanity check on the magnitude of your answer is worth the few seconds it takes.

solved.problem: Numeric Entry. If 3x − 7 = 20, enter the value of x.
solved.solution: 3x = 27, so x = 9. Enter 9 in the box.

solved.problem: Numeric Entry (fraction box). A recipe uses 2 cups of flour for every 3 cups of water. Enter the ratio of flour to water as a fraction.
solved.solution: The ratio is 2 to 3, so enter 2 in the numerator and 3 in the denominator: 2/3. (No need to reduce anything here.)

solved.problem: Numeric Entry. A jacket originally $120 is discounted 35%. Enter the sale price in dollars.
Numeric Entry, round to the nearest integer. The average of 47, 52, 48 and 55 is what?
solved.solution: Sum = 47 + 52 + 48 + 55 = 202. Average = 202/4 = 50.5, which rounds to 51. Enter 51.

Numeric Entry (fraction box). Of 20 students, 12 passed. Enter the fraction who passed (you need not reduce).
hints: 12 in the numerator, 20 in the denominator.

unsolved.problem: Numeric Entry. What is 15% of 240?
Numeric Entry. If 2x − 9 = −5, enter x (the box accepts negatives if needed).

topics.name: Select-One vs Select-All
topics.details: The GRE has two visually similar but behaviourally different formats, and confusing them costs easy points. Standard multiple choice uses oval buttons and has exactly one correct answer — pick the single best. Multiple-Answer questions use square boxes and instruct you to "select one or more" or "indicate all", meaning the number of correct answers is not fixed: it could be one, several, or every option. The scoring is unforgiving — you must select every correct choice and no incorrect one to get credit, with no partial marks — so you cannot stop after finding the first true statement. Some Multiple-Answer questions helpfully tell you exactly how many to pick ("select two"), which narrows the search; most do not, and then you must evaluate every option on its own. The habit that saves you: notice the button shape and read the instruction line first, so you know whether you are hunting for one answer or auditing all of them.

solved.problem: Select-all. Which of the following are factors of 24? Indicate ALL that apply. (A) 3 (B) 5 (C) 6 (D) 8 (E) 9
solved.solution: Test each: 24/3 = 8 ✓, 24/5 is not an integer ✗, 24/6 = 4 ✓, 24/8 = 3 ✓, 24/9 is not an integer ✗. Correct: A, C and D.

solved.problem: Select-all. Which values of x satisfy x² = 16? (A) −4 (B) −2 (C) 2 (D) 4
solved.solution: x² = 16 gives x = 4 or x = −4. A single multiple-choice item would trap you into picking only 4; the square-box format signals that both roots count. Correct: A and D.

solved.problem: Select-all. Which of these numbers are prime? (A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 9 (D) 11 (E) 15
solved.solution: 1 is not prime (by definition), 2 is prime, 9 = 3×3 is not, 11 is prime, 15 = 3×5 is not. Correct: B and D.

solved.problem: Select-all. If n is an integer and 2 < n ≤ 6, which values can n take? (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 6 (E) 7
solved.solution: Strictly greater than 2 excludes 2; up to and including 6 includes 6; 7 is out of range. Correct: B, C and D. (Watch the strict vs inclusive endpoints.)

unsolved.problem: Select-all. Which are factors of 18? (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 6 (D) 9 (E) 12
Select-all. Which values satisfy x² = 25? (A) −5 (B) −1 (C) 1 (D) 5
hints: A square root has two signs.

unsolved.problem: Select-all. Which are prime? (A) 2 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 7 (E) 21
Select-all. If −3 ≤ n < 2 and n is an integer, which can n be? (A) −3 (B) −1 (C) 0 (D) 2
Select-all. Which of these are multiples of 6? (A) 12 (B) 18 (C) 20 (D) 30
hints: A multiple of 6 divides evenly by 6.

topics.name: Checking Every Option
topics.details: Because a Multiple-Answer question can have any number of correct choices and gives no partial credit, the only safe method is to evaluate every option independently — never stop at the first one that works, and never assume the correct answers cluster together. Treat each choice as its own true/false test against the condition, and mark it only if it genuinely qualifies. For questions phrased as a range ("which could be the value of..."), a smart shortcut is to find the smallest and largest values that satisfy the condition; every option between those two extremes then qualifies, and you can sweep them in one pass. Guard against two habits from ordinary multiple choice: the instinct to pick exactly one answer, and the instinct to pick a "best" answer — here there is no best, only every-correct-one. When the algebra sets a boundary (say x > 4), test the endpoint carefully to decide whether it is included, since a strict versus inclusive inequality changes which options make the cut.

solved.problem: Select-all. If x is an integer and 3x < 20, which of these could be x? (A) 4 (B) 6 (C) 7 (D) 10
solved.solution: 3x < 20 means x < 6.67. Test each: 4 ✓ (12 < 20), 6 ✓ (18 < 20), 7 ✗ (21 > 20), 10 ✗. Correct: A and B. Checking each prevents assuming 7 sneaks in.

solved.problem: Select-all. A number added to 5 gives a result greater than 8 and at most 12. Which could the number be? (A) 2 (B) 4 (C) 7 (D) 8
solved.solution: Condition: 8 < n + 5 ≤ 12, so 3 < n ≤ 7. Test: 2 ✗, 4 ✓, 7 ✓ (endpoint included), 8 ✗. Correct: B and C.

solved.problem: Select-all. Which of these could be the length of the third side of a triangle with sides 6 and 10? (A) 3 (B) 5 (C) 12 (D) 16
solved.solution: The third side lies strictly between 10 − 6 = 4 and 10 + 6 = 16, i.e. 4 < side < 16. Test: 3 ✗, 5 ✓, 12 ✓, 16 ✗ (must be strictly less than 16). Correct: B and C.

solved.problem: Select-all. If 0 < x < 1, which of the following must be true? (A) x² < x (B) 1/x > 1 (C) x³ > x (D) √x > x
solved.solution: For a proper fraction: x² < x ✓; 1/x > 1 ✓; x³ > x is false (x³ < x) ✗; √x > x ✓. Correct: A, B and D. Each option is a separate must-be-true test.

unsolved.problem: Select-all. If x is an integer and 2x < 15, which could x be? (A) 5 (B) 7 (C) 8 (D) 10
Select-all. A number n satisfies 4 ≤ n + 1 < 9. Which could n be? (A) 3 (B) 5 (C) 7 (D) 8
Select-all. Third side of a triangle with sides 5 and 9? (A) 3 (B) 4 (C) 10 (D) 14
Select-all. If −2 < x < 3, which must be true? (A) x² < 9 (B) x > 0 (C) x + 2 > 0 (D) x is an integer
hints: x could be negative or non-integer.

topics.name: On-Screen Calculator & Estimation
topics.details: The GRE supplies an on-screen basic calculator — four operations, a square root, a percent key and a memory, and nothing more. It has no exponent, sine, or graphing functions, so it will not rescue a badly set-up problem; it only speeds up arithmetic you have already reasoned out. The strategic skill is knowing when NOT to use it. For Quantitative Comparison and for multiple choice with widely spaced answers, estimation is faster and less error-prone: round to friendly numbers and see which choice you land near. Reserve the calculator for messy exact arithmetic, especially on Numeric Entry where there are no choices to check against. Two cautions: transcribe carefully, since a mistyped digit produces a confidently wrong answer with no options to flag it, and mind the calculator’s display limits and order of operations — it will not respect implied grouping, so compute a bracketed expression in the right sequence yourself. Estimate first to know roughly what the answer should be, then let the calculator confirm the precise figure only when precision is actually required.

solved.problem: Multiple choice with choices 18, 20, 24, 30. Estimate 19% of 106 to pick the answer.
solved.solution: Round: 19% ≈ 20% and 106 ≈ 100, so ≈ 20% of 100 = 20. The nearest choice is 20 — no calculator needed. (Exact is 20.14.)
This is where the calculator earns its keep. Using the square-root key, √784 = 28 (since 28² = 784). Enter 28.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Quantity A: 48% of 250. Quantity B: 130. Estimate to answer.
solved.solution: 48% ≈ 50%, and 50% of 250 = 125, which is below 130 — but 48% is a touch under 50%, so Quantity A is even smaller, about 120. So Quantity A < 130: Quantity B is greater. Estimation settles it without exact multiplication.

solved.problem: Numeric Entry. A store sells 1,240 items at $37 each. Enter the total revenue in dollars.
solved.solution: Estimate first: 1,240 × 37 ≈ 1,200 × 37 ≈ 44,400, so the answer is around $46,000. Now use the calculator for the exact figure: 1,240 × 37 = 45,880. Enter 45880. (The estimate confirms you did not mistype.)

Numeric Entry. Enter √576.
QC estimate. Quantity A: 32% of 400. Quantity B: 120. Which is greater?
Numeric Entry. 2,050 × 48 — estimate first, then give the exact product.
Choices 6, 8, 12, 15. Estimate 24.6 ÷ 3.1.

shortcuts: Numeric Entry has no choices — you cannot back-solve, so set up carefully and sanity-check the magnitude of your answer.
In a fraction box you need not reduce: 6/8 scores exactly like 3/4, so skip the simplification.
Button shape tells you the format: ovals = pick one; squares = "select one or more".
Multiple-Answer is all-or-nothing — evaluate every option independently and never stop at the first hit.
For range-type select-all questions, find the smallest and largest qualifying values, then include everything between.
Estimate on Quantitative Comparison and widely spaced multiple choice; reserve the calculator for exact, messy arithmetic.
The on-screen calculator is basic (no exponents/trig) — it speeds arithmetic but never fixes a bad setup.
mistakes: Selecting only one answer on a square-box "select all" question when several are correct.
Stopping after the first correct option instead of auditing every choice.
Wasting simplification time reducing a fraction-box answer that need not be reduced.
Forgetting negative roots on a select-all (x² = 16 has both 4 and −4).
Mistyping a digit into the calculator and trusting the result — Numeric Entry has no choices to catch it.
Reaching for the calculator on a comparison a quick estimate would have settled faster.
Ignoring the rounding or units instruction ("to the nearest integer", "in dollars") on Numeric Entry.

pyq.q: A Numeric Entry answer is 3/4 but you compute 9/12. Do you need to reduce before entering?
pyq.a: No. Fraction boxes accept unreduced fractions, and 9/12 is scored the same as 3/4. Reducing is optional.

pyq.q: How do you know a GRE question wants more than one answer?
pyq.a: The choices sit in square boxes and the instruction says "select one or more" or "indicate all". Ovals mean exactly one answer.

pyq.q: On a select-all question, is there partial credit?
pyq.a: No. You must mark every correct choice and no incorrect one to earn the point — check each option before submitting.

pyq.q: When should you skip the on-screen calculator?
pyq.a: On Quantitative Comparison and multiple choice with far-apart answers — estimate by rounding. Use the calculator mainly for exact Numeric Entry arithmetic.

pyq.q: A select-all asks which values satisfy x² = 49. What is the trap?
pyq.a: Selecting only 7 and missing −7. The square-box format signals that both roots of the equation count.

Fraction boxes need not be reduced; enter the numerator and denominator you have and move on.
Square boxes mean "select one or more" — the number of correct answers ranges from one to all.
Multiple-Answer is all-or-nothing, so evaluate every option independently and never stop at the first hit.
For range-based select-all questions, bracket the min and max that qualify and include everything between.
